title: Random processes, spectra and random fields: from one velocity record to the energy spectrum
status: reviewed and locally validated; passes 1-9 complete; gate 6b passed round 3 (0 blocking)

Source of the adapted exercises T1-P5 and T1-P6, Exercises 8 and 9; no chapter section is grounded in this recording.

source_uncertainties: Spoken slip (L21 888-893 s): 'because they have the same one-time pdf, they have the same autocorrelation function' for processes (d) and (e). The slides (L20 f0039, L21 f0027) state that (d) and (e) have the same autocorrelation exp(-|s|/tau_bar) and (e) the same spectrum as (d); the reader text states the correct logic (same autocovariance if and only if same spectrum, by the Fourier pair).
Spoken speculation (L21 669-673 s) that process (b) is 'probably at a higher Reynolds number': not in the slide caption; omitted from reader text.

Spoken term 'Kronecker delta' (L22 about 1579, 1647, 1680 s) for the delta in the energy-spectrum definition; the slide (L22 f0046) writes delta(|kappa| - kappa) with a continuous argument, a Dirac delta. Reader text follows the slide and notes the difference.
Slide misprint (L22 f0006): the lower limit of the mean-velocity integral prints as infinity, not minus infinity; reader text notes it.
Slide notation (L22 f0031): L11 integral written with bold dr; the integration variable is the scalar separation r; reader text notes it.
Slide typo (T1 f0082): 'autocovaiance' for autocovariance; not mentioned in reader text.
Slide figure caption (L20 f0021, Figure 3.20): '(see Chapter 12)' refers to a chapter of the slides' source book, not of this book; omitted from reader text.

Slide figures 3.19 and 3.21 (L20 f0004, f0031): the sample paths of Fig. 3.19 spread between about 1.5 and 5.5 after the transient, whereas the right axis of Fig. 3.21 gives a variance of about 0.065; the two appear inconsistent (a spread of that width suggests a variance of order 0.5-1). The chapter uses Fig. 3.21 only qualitatively (mean and variance become constant after about t = 6).
Slide value (L21 f0041, Figure 3.24): kurtosis 11 of the second derivative of the turbulent velocity (process a); attributed to the slide in reader text, not verified against a source.

Symbol T on the slides has three meanings: time shift in the stationarity definition (L20 f0004, L22 f0014), period of a periodic process (L20 f0024), record length (T1 f0095). Reader text uses t_s (shift, as chapter 6), T_p (period) and T (record length), and states this once.
Spoken (L22 1141-1150, 1203-1205 s): the lecturer uses k and kappa interchangeably for the wavenumber; the slides write kappa. Reader text uses kappa and keeps k for the turbulent kinetic energy.

Isotropy slide (L22 f0027) writes the transformed position and velocity with an overbar; this book reserves the overbar for the LES filtered velocity; reader text describes the transformation in words and points to chapter 6's direction cosines a_ij.

Running-case assumption: the integral time scale of the jet centreline velocity, tau_bar = 0.01 s, is assumed (of the order of ell_0 / <U_1> = 12.5 ms), not measured; every result that uses it is stated as proportional to it in reader text. Taylor's hypothesis is named only as a forward pointer.

Sources not obtainable by scripted download on 2026-10-05 and therefore not cited: G. I. Taylor (1938), 'The spectrum of turbulence', Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 164 (publisher and mirror returned HTTP 403); D. H. Lenschow, J. Mann, L. Kristensen (1994), J. Atmos. Ocean. Tech. 11 (AMS and UCAR OpenSky returned challenge pages).

Beyhaghi, Alimo and Bewley (arXiv:1802.01056): journal version not checked; arXiv preprint pages cited and marked as such in reader text. Lee and Moser (arXiv:1410.7809): the preprint states it was under consideration at J. Fluid Mech.; no published version checked; preprint pages cited and marked in reader text.

Practice problem L59-P7 part 2 needs <udot^2> > 0 for a strict inequality, and T1-P6's long-time step needs (1/T) int_0^T s rho(s) ds -> 0; both provisos are added in the solutions (practice-map.md notes).

ASR spellings corrected: 'Onsten-Ollenberg', 'austen all in the process' = Ornstein-Uhlenbeck; 'round's decomposition' = Reynolds decomposition; 'RFS', 'R of s' = R(s); 'phii' = Phi_ii; 'chronicle delta' = Kronecker delta (as spoken); 'statistically fully disruptive inflow' = statistically fully developed flow; '1.1 time' = one-point, one-time; 'endpoint end time' = N-point N-time; 'U2' (L20 264 s) = U(t); 'feels' (L22 282 s) = fields.

The name 'Wiener-Khinchin theorem' was removed in round 1 (no source in the repository); the chapter states the parts it uses and their condition (absolutely integrable R) and cites no general theorem.

Practice problem T1-P5: board frames f0087, f0088 and f0093 viewed in round 1. The corrected board work differentiates in t (product rule), drops the total t-derivative by stationarity and boxes B(s) = -d^2R/ds^2 (f0093); the chapter's solution takes a different route (change from differentiating the second factor to the first) to the same result.

The source-note statement that the slides of this module name one source (Pope 2000) rests on chapter 7's check of the Module 04 Source slide (L17, extracted frame at 238.5 s; chapter 7 meta), not on a frame of L20-L22; the slides of L20-L22 carry the same Module 04 header and sidebar entry 'Source'.

Timestamps are section anchors from local speech-recognition segment times; they locate topic changes to within a few seconds. The section spanning the end of L21 and the start of L22 was split in round 1, so every timestamp now sits in a heading.

sections.section: The objects of the chapter and the running case
sections.lecture_material: None directly; extends chapter 7's repeatable experiment.
sections.teaching_construction: Random process as a family of random variables indexed by t; sample path; hot-wire record on the jet centreline of chapters 6-7 (mean 8 m/s, rms 2 m/s, ell_0 = 0.1 m, tau_eta = 0.43 ms, 20 kHz); assumed tau_bar = 0.01 s; symbol decisions s, t_s, x_s, T, T_p.

sections.section: A velocity recorded in time is a random process
sections.lecture_material: U(t) as a random process; one-time CDF F(V,t) and PDF f(V;t); no joint information at two times; N-time CDF and complete characterization (almost impossible); Figure 3.19 (three sample paths); Figure 3.20 (five processes a-e with the same standardized Gaussian one-time PDF).
sections.teaching_construction: Semicolon convention stated; N = 2 reduction to chapter 7's joint CDF (7.14).

sections.section: Statistical stationarity
sections.lecture_material: Stationarity: multi-time statistics invariant under a shift in time; many turbulent flows stationary after an initial transient; flow variables vary, statistics do not.
sections.research_extension: Beyhaghi, Alimo, Bewley 2018 (arXiv p. 5): procedures to identify the initial transient; tests of second-order stationarity.
sections.teaching_construction: One- and two-time consequences of (8.3); examples of non-stationary flows; jet assumption; chapter 7 Lorenz-ensemble variances 57.8 and 61.6 as an undecided case.

sections.section: Statistical stationarity (continued)
sections.lecture_material: Figure 3.21: mean and variance of the process of Figure 3.19 constant after the transient.
sections.teaching_construction: As above.

sections.section: Autocovariance, autocorrelation function and integral time scale
sections.lecture_material: R(s) and rho(s); properties rho(0) = 1, |rho| <= 1, even; periodicity; integral time scale tau_bar = int_0^inf rho ds, converging because correlation diminishes with lag.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of the bound from chapter 7's Cauchy-Schwarz argument and of evenness from a stationary shift; convergence of (8.6) as an assumption with counterexamples (1/(1+|s|), constant, cos s); exponential example (8.7) with running-case values; cutoff in estimating tau_bar (code: 0.989, 0.985 vs 0.993).

sections.section: What the autocorrelation distinguishes, and what it does not
sections.lecture_material: Figure 3.22 (autocorrelations of a-e; a and c smooth at origin; b narrower; d and e exp(-|s|/tau_bar)); all except b share tau_bar; one-time PDF and autocorrelation do not characterize a process.
sections.teaching_construction: Computed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and jump processes with identical one-time PDF and autocorrelation; derivation of the jump-process autocorrelation and of the increment flatness 3/p = 61.5 (measured 62.0); Figure 8.1 from the listing's arrays.

sections.section: The frequency spectrum and the autocovariance form a Fourier pair
sections.lecture_material: E(omega) = (1/pi) int R e^{-i omega s} ds = (2/pi) int_0^inf R cos; R(s) = (1/2) int E e^{i omega s} = int_0^inf E cos; 'twice the frequency spectrum' forms the pair; R and E real and even, same information; spectral representation as a sum of Fourier modes.
sections.teaching_construction: Statement of the convention (one-sided, angular frequency, factor 2pi per Hz); exponential-Lorentzian pair (8.10) with checks and running-case values (E(0) = 0.0255 m^2/s, 15.9 Hz); code spectra at three frequencies. Existence condition for (8.8): absolutely integrable R; the constant and periodic processes as excluded cases; sin(s)/s derived from a band-limited spectrum by (8.9) as a finite tau_bar without absolute integrability.

sections.section: The frequency spectrum and the autocovariance form a Fourier pair (recap)
sections.lecture_material: Recap of the Fourier pair and its cosine forms.
sections.teaching_construction: As above.

sections.section: The spectrum distributes the variance over frequencies
sections.lecture_material: R(0) = <u^2> = int_0^inf E d omega; band contribution (fundamental property); tau_bar = pi E(0)/(2<u^2>) derived on the board; process b smaller tau_bar and E(0), extends to higher frequencies; Figure 3.23 (spectra); one-time PDF and autocorrelation only a partial characterization.
sections.teaching_construction: Expected periodogram (8.12) and non-negativity of E; derivative variance (8.14) from difference quotients and its spectral form; smoothness at the origin versus existence of a derivative; Ornstein-Uhlenbeck difference quotients in the code (9.1, 19.0, 39.1). Limit in (8.14) by dominated convergence (finite case) and Fatou's lemma (infinite case).

sections.section: Time averages, ergodicity and the length of a record
sections.lecture_material: None in L20-L22 (the practice problem T1-P6, Exercise 9, states the central formula).
sections.research_extension: Beyhaghi, Alimo, Bewley 2018 (arXiv): p. 1 stationarity and ergodicity generally assumed for turbulence statistics; p. 2 eq. (1b) averaging-error model attributed to Lumley and Panofsky (1964); p. 3 validity for large T/tau_f and sampling interval 2 tau_f / c, c of order 10; p. 6 eq. (6) discrete form.
sections.teaching_construction: Time average (8.15); exact variance (8.16); long-time form (8.17) with its conditions; exact exponential form (8.18); link to E(0) (8.19); mean-square ergodicity and the sufficient condition int |R| < inf; running-case record lengths (0.28 m/s for 1 s; 12.5 s for 1 %; proportional to tau_bar); code: 0.0383 and 0.0381 vs 0.0392, naive 0.0010.

sections.section: The stationary Gaussian process, and why a turbulent velocity is not one
sections.lecture_material: Gaussian process: N-time PDF joint normal, characterized by means and covariances; stationary case characterized by mean, variance and rho; process c Gaussian with the spectrum of a; Figure 3.24 (second derivatives); kurtosis 3 for c and 11 for a; do not approximate a turbulent velocity by a Gaussian process.
sections.research_extension: Backward reference to chapter 7 (Wilczek et al. 2011; Kerr 1983 derivative flatness 3.39-5.11).
sections.teaching_construction: General N-dimensional normal density (8.20) and its N = 2 reduction to (7.22); conditions (stationarity, mean) for characterization by the spectrum; equal second-order derivative statistics of a and c; boundary of the lecture's warning by the order of the statistic.

sections.section: Random fields: the one-point, one-time PDF
sections.lecture_material: Velocity as a time-dependent random vector field; one-point one-time joint CDF and PDF (triple derivative); semicolon notation; no joint information at two points or times.
sections.teaching_construction: Units of the PDF; chapter 7's joint and one-component PDFs as marginals of the one-point PDF; what a one- or two-component probe at the jet station measures.

sections.section: Mean, fluctuation, Reynolds stresses and the N-point PDF
sections.lecture_material: Mean velocity field, fluctuation, Reynolds decomposition, Reynolds stresses; differentiability (mean of derivative = derivative of mean); N-point N-time PDF impossible to determine; turbulent fields not Gaussian.
sections.teaching_construction: Condition for interchanging mean and derivative linked to (8.14); slide misprint noted.

sections.section: Stationarity and homogeneity of a field, and the channel flow
sections.lecture_material: Stationarity and homogeneity in terms of the N-point PDF; homogeneous U implies uniform mean, zero in a suitable frame; homogeneous turbulence (fluctuation homogeneous) less restrictive, wind tunnels and DNS; Figure 3.25 channel: statistically 2D for b/h >> 1, |x3|/b << 1, 1D for x1/h >> 1.
sections.research_extension: Lee and Moser 2014 (arXiv:1410.7809): periodic x and z, domain 8 pi delta by 3 pi delta (p. 3); U(y) (p. 4); LM5200 run time 7.80 delta/u_tau without transition (Table 1, p. 4); sampling uncertainty (method of Oliver et al., named in the meta only) < 0.2 % mean, < 0.5 % near-wall and 3 % outer variances (p. 4); stationarity test via linear total stress (p. 5).
sections.teaching_construction: Independence of stationarity and homogeneity; linear mean compatible with homogeneous fluctuations; approximations versus exact properties; jet stationary but not homogeneous.

sections.section: Isotropy
sections.lecture_material: Homogeneous field invariant under translations; isotropic if also invariant under rotations and reflections; example <u1^2> = <u2^2> = <u3^2>; importance in experiments and theory; N-point PDF statement.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of <u_i u_j> = (2/3) k delta_ij from one reflection and one rotation; scope (shear flows, jet centreline test, local isotropy of chapter 5).

sections.section: The two-point correlation and the integral length scale
sections.lecture_material: Two-point one-time autocovariance R_ij(r,x,t); integral length scale L11; independence of x for homogeneous turbulence.
sections.teaching_construction: Symmetry R_ij(r) = R_ji(-r) derived from homogeneity; L11 as the spatial counterpart of tau_bar; link to chapter 5's integral scale; single-probe limitation and forward pointer to Taylor's hypothesis.

sections.section: Wavenumber spectra: the velocity-spectrum tensor and the energy spectrum
sections.lecture_material: Fourier mode, wavelength 2 pi/|kappa|; Phi_ij and R_ij Fourier pair with (2 pi)^-3; r = 0 gives Reynolds stresses; two kinds of directional information; energy-spectrum function with delta(|kappa| - kappa); integral of E gives k.
sections.teaching_construction: Normalization compared with (8.8)-(8.9); units of Phi and E; reality of Phi_ii from evenness of R_ii; derivation of (8.33) from (8.31); isotropic shell formula E = 2 pi kappa^2 Phi_ii (8.34); distinction between E(omega) and E(kappa,t).

sections.section: Executable processes: two processes with the same autocorrelation
sections.lecture_material: Processes (d) and (e) of Figure 3.20 motivate the pair.
sections.teaching_construction: NumPy program (seed 8): Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (exact AR(1) sampling) and jump process with identical one-time PDF and autocorrelation; moments, autocorrelation, integral time scale, time-average variance vs (8.18), periodogram vs (8.10), increment flatness, OU difference quotients; four assertions (two per process); failure test (jump probability 0.5) fails the autocorrelation assertion.

sections.section: What the description establishes and what it does not
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Classification of definitions, derived results and assumptions; conventions; scope of second-order descriptions; dependence of running-case numbers on the assumed tau_bar.

sections.section: Exercises
sections.lecture_material: Exercises 7-9 are adapted from the course practice problems L59-P7 (iX5PG6TPABQ 0:06), T1-P5 (fgMG7Jd89pw 40:28) and T1-P6 (fgMG7Jd89pw 46:59), as assigned by _editorial/practice-map.md.
sections.research_extension: Exercise 1(c) uses Beyhaghi et al. p. 3.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises (compute, counterexample, check an assumption, derive, judge a claim, derive and judge) and full solutions for all nine.

references.title: Beyhaghi, Alimo, Bewley 2018, A multiscale, asymptotically unbiased approach to uncertainty quantification in the numerical approximation of infinite time-averaged statistics (arXiv:1802.01056v1)
references.supports: p. 1 (abstract): 'the statistics of many turbulent flows are generally considered as stationary and ergodic after some initial transient is identified and set aside'. p. 2: eq. (1b) epsilon_hat(T) = sigma sqrt(2 tau_f / T), 'tau_f is a modeling parameter, referred to as the integral time scale'; model attributed to [20] = Lumley and Panofsky, The structure of atmospheric turbulence (1964) (reference list). p. 3: 'This model is found to be effective in practice only if the simulation time divided by the integral time scale, T/tau_f, is relatively large'; h = 2 tau_f / c with c of order 10; 'sampling substantially more frequently than this will not substantially reduce epsilon(T)'. p. 5: identification of the initial transient; second-order stationarity tests (Priestley-Subba-Rao, wavelet spectrum). p. 6: eq. (6) epsilon_s^2 = (sigma^2/s)[1 + 2 sum (1 - k/s) rho(k)].
references.page_checked: arXiv preprint pp. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 (PDF pp. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6); reference list PDF pp. 18-20; journal version not checked

references.title: Lee and Moser 2014, Direct numerical simulation of turbulent channel flow up to Re_tau = 5200 (arXiv:1410.7809v1)
references.supports: p. 1: 'Under consideration for publication in J. Fluid Mech.'. p. 3: 'Periodic boundary conditions are applied in the streamwise (x) and spanwise (z) directions, and no-slip/no-penetration boundary conditions are applied at the wall. The computational domain sizes are Lx = 8 pi delta and Lz = 3 pi delta, where delta is the channel half-width'. p. 4: 'U(y) is the mean streamwise velocity'; Table 1: LM5200 Re_tau = 5186, T u_tau / delta = 7.80 ('Total simulation time without transition'); 'the estimated standard deviation of mean velocity is less than 0.2% and the estimated standard deviation of variance and covariance of the velocity components is less than 0.5% in near-wall region (y+ < 100 say) and 3% in outer-region (y > 0.2 delta say)', method of Oliver et al. (2014). p. 5: stationarity tested with the total stress, linear in a statistically stationary channel (eq. 2.1).
